description: Semantic elements that describe meaning — and why they matter for accessibility.

screens.body:
Most HTML tags describe what content MEANS, not what it looks like:

means "main heading",

means "paragraph", means "link". Tags with built-in meaning are called semantic. They're the opposite of generic boxes like

that say nothing about their contents. Writing semantic HTML means choosing the tag that matches the content's role. Browsers, search engines, and assistive tech all read that meaning.

options: Tags that describe the content's meaning
check.question: What does "semantic HTML" mean?

screens.heading: Tags that mean something
screens.keyPoint: Semantic tags describe content's role; <div> describes nothing.

screens.body:
The classic page landmarks: <header> (top: logo, site name), <nav> (navigation links), <main> (the page's primary content), <footer> (bottom: copyright, contact).

These create a map of the page. Screen-reader users can jump straight to <main> and skip the menu — but only if you use the tags.

One rule: exactly one <main> per page. Headers and footers can repeat (an <article> can have its own <header>), but the page has a single main act.

check.question: Which set marks up a page's landmarks semantically?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: page landmarks -->
<header>
  <nav><!-- links --></nav>
</header>
<main><!-- the page's core content --></main>
<footer><!-- copyright, contact --></footer>

screens.heading: Landmarks: header, nav, main, footer
screens.keyPoint: Landmarks map the page. Exactly one <main>; screen readers jump between landmarks.

screens.body:
<article> is for self-contained content: a blog post, a news story, a product card — something that makes sense on its own.

<section> groups related content under a theme: "Pricing plans", "Reviews". A section usually starts with a heading.

Quick test: would this chunk make sense copied onto another page alone? Yes → <article>. Is it just a themed grouping → <section>.

check.question: A blog post with its own title and author — which tag?

code.snippet:
Latest posts

My Calgary weekend

New gig posted

screens.heading: Article vs section
screens.keyPoint: <article> = stands alone. <section> = themed grouping, usually with a heading.

screens.body:
<aside> is for content related to its surroundings but not central: sidebars, pull quotes, "related articles" boxes, ad slots.

Where you place it changes its meaning: inside an <article>, it's related to that article; outside, it's related to the whole page.

Screen readers may announce it as complementary content, so keep it genuinely secondary — not the punchline of the page.

check.question: A "Related gigs" sidebar next to a task page — which tag?

code.snippet: Related gigs

screens.heading: Aside: the sidekick
screens.keyPoint: <aside> = related-but-secondary content: sidebars, related links, pull quotes.

screens.body:
Here's why all this matters beyond tidy code: accessibility. Millions of people browse with screen readers, keyboards only, or voice control.

A screen reader user hears your landmarks announced: "navigation", "main", "complementary". With div-soup, they hear "div, div, div" — a maze with no signs.

Semantic HTML is the cheapest accessibility win there is: no extra tools, no plugins — just choosing the right tag.

options: It announces landmarks so they can jump to "main" directly
It makes the page load faster
check.question: How does semantic HTML help a screen-reader user?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: a map, not a maze -->
<!-- Screen reader hears: -->
<!-- "banner, navigation, main, contentinfo" -->
<header>…</header>
<nav>…</nav>
<main>…</main>
<footer>…</footer>

screens.heading: Why it matters: accessibility
screens.keyPoint: Landmarks become navigation for assistive tech. Div-soup is a maze with no signs.

screens.body:
Two accessibility habits that pair with semantics. First, alt text on images (from the text & media lesson) — specific descriptions, empty alt="" for decoration.

Second, connected labels on form inputs — label's for matches input's id, so screen readers announce what each field is.

Also: keep heading order logical (no jumping from h1 to h4) and make sure everything works with a keyboard — if you can Tab to it and Enter activates it, you're on the right track.

options: label's for matching the input's id
A placeholder with an example value
check.question: What tells a screen reader what a form field is for?

screens.heading: Accessibility habits to pair with it
screens.keyPoint: Alt text + connected labels + logical heading order = accessible by default.

screens.body:
So when DO you use <div>? For pure styling hooks — grouping things so CSS can lay them out, with no meaning attached.

<span> is div's inline sibling: for styling a few words inside a paragraph.

That's the whole rule: if the wrapper MEANS something, there's probably a semantic tag for it. If it's just a box for styling, <div> is perfect.

options: A wrapper that exists only so CSS can style it
check.question: When is <div> the right choice?

screens.heading: Div's honest job
screens.keyPoint: <div> = styling-only wrapper. If the content means something, use a semantic tag.
